header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care
guidelineVersions: NHS AAA screening programme overview (updated May 2026)

related.why: Another vascular emergency needing a regional vascular service

brief.setting: Emergency department of a district general hospital without on-site vascular surgery
brief.scenario: Mr Graham Pollard, 74, collapsed at home with sudden severe back and left loin pain. He smokes and has hypertension. He is pale and sweaty but talking. Pulse 118, BP 84/50. He has a 5.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm, measured on a surveillance scan 4 months ago.
brief.task: The examiner will ask you about your assessment and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Suspected rupture: confirm quickly, call the vascular centre early, keep him conscious, not normotensive, and move him fast.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling it renal colic, or pouring in crystalloid to 'normalise' his blood pressure.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is a ruptured aneurysm until proven otherwise. ABCDE, and I'll call my senior."

grid.label: Recognition
grid.fail: Diagnoses renal colic or a musculoskeletal back pain.
grid.pass: Suspects rupture: new back or abdominal pain with collapse, in a man over 60 who smokes, with hypertension and a known AAA.
grid.high: Knows ruptures often mimic renal colic, and that a small aneurysm under surveillance can still rupture.

grid.label: Resuscitation and blood
grid.fail: Gives litres of crystalloid and forgets blood.
grid.pass: ABCDE, oxygen, two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch; activates the major haemorrhage protocol; senior surgeon and anaesthetist informed.
grid.high: Uses blood and products rather than crystalloid, with plasma to red cells close to 1:1, as ESVS suggests.

grid.label: Permissive hypotension (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Aims for a normal blood pressure.
grid.pass: Restrictive volume resuscitation: tolerates a low pressure while he stays conscious and talking.
grid.high: Gives the ESVS target: conscious, systolic 70–90 mmHg; knows IMPROVE data suggest 70 may be too low in ruptured AAA.

grid.label: Imaging
grid.fail: Sends him round the department for a CT before calling anyone.
grid.pass: Immediate bedside ultrasound; discusses immediately with the regional vascular service, even if ultrasound is unavailable or non-diagnostic.
grid.high: CT angiography only if the vascular team wants it for planning and he is stable enough; the unstable may go straight to theatre.

grid.label: Transfer decision and timing
grid.fail: Delays transfer to calculate a risk score or complete tests.
grid.pass: Once accepted, he leaves within 30 minutes of the transfer decision, with the transfer protocol.
grid.high: Knows no single sign or score decides transfer; cardiac arrest or persistent loss of consciousness means negligible chance of surviving repair.

grid.label: EVAR or open repair
grid.pass: Consider EVAR or open repair for ruptured infrarenal AAA; open if EVAR is anatomically unsuitable.
grid.high: EVAR benefits most, especially men over 70 and women of any age; open may suit men under 70; EVAR under local anaesthetic.

grid.label: Complications after repair
grid.fail: Thinks the job ends in theatre.
grid.pass: Watches for abdominal compartment syndrome if he doesn't improve after repair.
grid.high: Also colonic ischaemia (bloody diarrhoea, acidosis): flexible sigmoidoscopy to confirm.

grid.label: Communication and ceilings of care
grid.fail: Doesn't involve the family or discuss what happens if he isn't a candidate.
grid.pass: Tells him and his family what is happening; if the vascular team declines repair, plans end-of-life care.
grid.high: Makes the decision with the vascular consultant, not on a single sign; documents the plan and times.

fail.text: What do you think is going on?

fail.text: Loin pain radiating to the groin: renal colic. I'd give him analgesia and send a urine dip.

fail.text: I'll let the vascular centre talk to her.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What do you think is going on?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A ruptured aneurysm until proven otherwise: back pain and collapse, known AAA, smoker, hypertensive, over 60.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ABCDE, oxygen, two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol. I'd tell my registrar and the anaesthetist.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd restrict fluids and accept a low pressure as long as he stays conscious and talking.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What do you think is going on?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Ruptured AAA until proven otherwise. Back pain and collapse in a hypertensive smoker with a known aneurysm. It often mimics renal colic, and 5.1 cm doesn't mean it can't rupture.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: ABCDE, high-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch and major haemorrhage protocol. Blood and plasma close to 1:1 rather than crystalloid. Registrar, consultant and anaesthetist now; nothing like an arterial line should delay him.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Permissive hypotension: he's talking, so his brain is perfused. ESVS suggests keeping him conscious with a systolic of 70 to 90; in an older man I wouldn't let it drift below 70.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Bedside ultrasound in resus, and I'm phoning the vascular centre at the same time. CT angiography only if they want it for planning and he's stable enough; if not, he goes straight to their theatre.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Out of the door within 30 minutes of that decision. No risk score decides this. It would only change if he arrested or lost consciousness and stayed that way.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: For an infrarenal rupture, EVAR gives most benefit, especially in men over 70 like him, and can be done under local anaesthetic. Open repair if his anatomy isn't suitable.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: After repair, abdominal compartment syndrome if he isn't improving, and colonic ischaemia: bloody diarrhoea means a flexible sigmoidoscopy.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd tell him and his wife honestly how serious this is. The repair decision is the vascular consultant's, and I'd document times and decisions.

failures.move: Running in crystalloid to restore a normal blood pressure.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: raising the pressure and diluting clotting factors can restart bleeding from the contained rupture.

failures.move: Sending him for CT before speaking to the vascular centre.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: an unstable patient may arrest in the scanner, and transfer is delayed.

failures.move: Using a risk score to decide whether he is worth transferring.
failures.consequence: NICE says no score determines transfer and scores must not decide on repair; it delays transfer and may deny a survivable repair.

failures.move: Diagnosing renal colic in an older man with loin pain and hypotension.
failures.consequence: He is sent to the wrong pathway while he bleeds.

recovery.when: You gave a fluid bolus by reflex
recovery.line: I'd stop there: permissive hypotension, blood not crystalloid, as long as he's talking.

recovery.when: You can't recall the EVAR criteria
recovery.line: That's the vascular centre's decision; my job is to get him there within 30 minutes.

knowledge.fact: Suspect rupture with new abdominal or back pain, collapse or loss of consciousness; more likely with a known AAA, age over 60, smoking or hypertension.
Accepted for transfer: leave within 30 minutes. Consider permissive hypotension during transfer.
Permissive hypotension: conscious and able to speak, systolic 70–90 mmHg. Plasma to red cells close to 1:1.
Screening: men in the year they turn 65.
Refer 5.5 cm or more within 2 weeks; 3.0–5.4 cm within 12 weeks. Elective repair: consider if symptomatic, 5.5 cm or more, or over 4.0 cm and grown over 1 cm in a year.
Suspected colonic ischaemia after repair: flexible sigmoidoscopy.

recall.say: "Ruptured AAA until proven otherwise: call the vascular centre now."
do: Major haemorrhage protocol; blood, not crystalloid

numbers.meaning: leave the referring unit after the transfer decision
refer within 2 weeks; consider elective repair

recall.trap: 'Renal colic' in an older hypotensive man.
recall.finish: EVAR, or open repair if EVAR is unsuitable.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

sources.name: NICE NG156: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: diagnosis and management
sources.supports: Refer AAA 5.5 cm or larger to a regional vascular service to be seen within 2 weeks; 3.0-5.4 cm within 12 weeks (1.1.5, for AAAs found on ultrasound); think of rupture with new abdominal and/or back pain, cardiovascular collapse or loss of consciousness, more likely with known AAA, age over 60, smoking or hypertension (1.1.7); immediate bedside aortic ultrasound, and discuss immediately with a regional vascular service if it shows an AAA or is unavailable or non-diagnostic (1.1.9); consider CT angiography for suspected rupture being evaluated for repair (1.1.12); no single symptom, sign or risk tool determines transfer (1.3.1); cardiac arrest and/or persistent loss of consciousness: negligible chance of surviving repair (1.3.2); care of dying adults if repair inappropriate (1.3.3); leave the referring unit within 30 minutes of the decision to transfer (1.3.4); consider permissive hypotension during transfer (1.3.6); no scoring systems to decide on repair (1.4.4-1.4.5); unruptured: consider repair if symptomatic, 5.5 cm or more, or over 4.0 cm and grown over 1 cm in a year (1.5.1); ruptured infrarenal: consider EVAR or open repair; EVAR more benefit for most, especially men over 70 and women of any age; open likely better for men under 70 (1.6.1); open if standard EVAR unsuitable (1.6.2); consider local anaesthetic alone for EVAR (1.6.4); abdominal compartment syndrome after repair (1.6.5-1.6.6)

sources.name: Wanhainen A, Van Herzeele I, Bastos Goncalves F, et al. European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) 2024 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-Iliac Artery Aneurysms. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2024;67:192-331
sources.supports: Prompt CT angiography for suspected rupture (Rec 70); most who reach hospital alive are stable enough for CTA; the too unstable may go straight to theatre; haemodynamic instability = loss or reduced consciousness or systolic BP under 80 mmHg; permissive hypotension recommended (Rec 72), e.g. restricting fluids, with consciousness and the ability to speak as markers of cerebral perfusion; text: patient conscious with a target systolic 70-90 mmHg, and IMPROVE suggested 70 mmHg may be too low; resuscitate with blood and products, plasma to red cells close to 1:1; local anaesthesia for EVAR (Rec 73); EVAR first option for rupture with suitable anatomy (Rec 80); monitor intra-abdominal pressure after repair for abdominal compartment syndrome (Rec 81) and decompressive laparotomy if it develops (Rec 82); ureteric colic and myocardial infarction are the most common misdiagnoses; flexible sigmoidoscopy if colonic ischaemia suspected after repair (Rec 84)

sources.name: NHS England: Abdominal aortic aneurysm screening programme overview (GOV.UK)
sources.supports: Screening offered to men in the screening year they turn 65, by ultrasound; not routinely offered to women or men under 65; men over 65 not invited can self-refer

media.task: Say what the bedside scan shows and what you would do next
media.description: Transverse bedside ultrasound of the abdominal aorta showing an aneurysm of about 5-6 cm with calipers; optional

partner.opening: Mr Pollard has just arrived by ambulance. What do you think is going on, and how would you manage him?

reveals.finding: Tender, pulsatile, expansile mass in the epigastrium; left loin bruising. Femoral pulses present.

reveals.trigger: Asks for bloods and a gas
reveals.finding: Hb 92 g/L, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 128 µmol/L. Crossmatch sent.
Infrarenal aorta 5.6 cm; free fluid can't be assessed. The vascular centre, 40 minutes away, accepts him.

reveals.trigger: Asks about the response to treatment
reveals.finding: After 2 units of red cells and 2 of plasma: BP 92/58, pulse 108, still talking.

push.question: What blood pressure are you aiming for?
push.expect: A restrictive approach: accept a low pressure while he stays conscious and talking; ESVS suggests systolic 70–90 mmHg.

push.question: How quickly should he leave, and what would stop you sending him?
push.expect: Within 30 minutes of the decision; no score decides; cardiac arrest or persistent loss of consciousness means negligible survival.

push.question: Which repair would you expect, and why?
push.expect: EVAR or open; EVAR gives most benefit, especially men over 70 and women; open if EVAR unsuitable.

curveballs.prompt: His wife asks why the aneurysm wasn't fixed at 5.1 cm.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain honestly that elective repair is usually considered at 5.5 cm, or earlier if it grows fast or causes symptoms, and that smaller ones can still rupture.

curveballs.prompt: He becomes unresponsive and pulseless before transfer.
curveballs.safeAnswer: ALS; if he arrests with a confirmed rupture, his chance of surviving repair is negligible; discuss with the vascular consultant and family.

curveballs.prompt: On day 1 after repair his bladder pressure is high, he is oliguric and hard to ventilate.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Abdominal compartment syndrome: tell the vascular team now; decompression may be needed.
